QUESTION OF THE WEEK - The RBA board meets on Tuesday. Although this week's cut means little attention will be paid to the meeting, the rate outlook is still interesting. Economists were asked what chance they put on a sixth rate cut this cycle, and what they saw as the most likely next move in rates. Briefly, a further cut was only seen as a 30 percent chance, with the next most likley move being a rate rise in the middle of next year. However a significant minority -- seven out of 29 -- see a strong chance of another easing in 1998.

LABOUR FORCE - One of the key factors behind the five rate cuts seen so far, not much good news is expected on the employment front in June, or even through the September quarter, given the lack of momentum in indicators such as retail trade and the housing sector.

While the median forecast of 25,000 would normally be considered strong growth, it would still leave employment negative over the last three months, and only growing at a rate of 3,000 jobs per month over the first seven months of 1997.

The breakdown between full and part-time employment will also be keenly watched. Full-time employment fell by almost 64,000 in the first half of the year, and further weakness would be a concern for policymakers, economists said.

Unemployment is expected to rise back above 8.5 percent after its dip in June, reflecting the stagnant conditions in the labour market. The participation rate is also expected to end three months of declines, with a reversal forecast of the drop in the rate in June.

HOUSING FINANCE - After a large fall in May, many were expecting a rebound in the June data. However, the Australian Bankers Association is suggesting another sizeable fall in June -- when new borrowers would have been able to take advantage of the May 23 cut in rates. Combined with the weakness in June retail trade, and what are expected to be softish employment data, a weak housing finance figure would be bullish for those looking for another interest rate cut.
